title: Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies — Frank Coyle, UC Berkeley
talk_summary: Frank Coyle argues that probabilistic LLM agents should be wrapped in symbolic guardrails (ontologies/knowledge graphs with RDFS/OWL constraints) so a validator can check tool outputs before they're accepted. He sketches the standard agent loop (call tool, inspect stop reason, validate result, retry or escalate) and places Pydantic at the input boundary and an ontology-based reasoner at the output boundary.

takeaways.technique: Ontology/reasoner as output validator in the agent loop
takeaways.what_they_do: After a tool runs, the result is formatted and passed to a validator built on domain ontology constraints (functional, disjoint, transitive properties) that decides whether the LLM's output is reasonable before it is accepted, otherwise it loops back or escalates to a human.
takeaways.evidence_quote: think about the validator as operating with this these ontologies about our domain, then we can make some sense of whether the response of the LLM is reasonable

takeaways.technique: Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger
takeaways.what_they_do: Type-check tool inputs with Pydantic schemas before execution, then check tool results against ontology constraints; agents are kept side-effect-free until validation passes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger, and pure agents ... your agents should try to have no side effects

takeaways.technique: Explicit stop-reason-driven loop with validation branch
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent loop inspects the model's stop reason; if it is tool_use, execute the tool, validate the result, and either continue, feed the failure back to the LLM, or bring in a human.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Call a tool, check the stop reason. If it's a reasonable result, then let's go with it. If it's not reasonable, go back to the LLM.

takeaways.technique: Reuse existing taxonomies instead of inventing schemas
takeaways.what_they_do: Recommends adopting established vocabularies (schema.org, FOAF, Dublin Core, DBpedia) rather than building domain ontologies from scratch.
Notes that loops can break, drift, and inflate token counts, so validation/guardrails should terminate or redirect loops rather than letting them run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Loops can drift as agents start talking to each other ... Token counts crank up as the loops continue.
